result.rationale: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is true, parseRefreshTokenResponse uses minimumTokenResponseSchema, which only guarantees access_token plus one numeric property; z.object strips unknown keys by default, so expires_in/expiry fields are dropped. In office365calendar CalendarService the code merges `{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...(tokenResponse.data) }`, so the old (already expired) expiry timestamp survives, causing a token refresh on every subsequent request — exactly the mechanism the finding describes. This is verifiable from the new parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts and the modified O365 merge

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that parseRefreshTokenResponse strips expires_in before Outlook merges credentials. Looking at the diff, parseRefreshTokenResponse (lines 12-29 of the new file) simply validates the response against a schema and adds a placeholder refresh_token if missing. It doesn't strip any fields - it returns the parsed data as-is. The minimumTokenResponseSchema allows any string key with number values and optional unknown properties, so expires_in would be preserved. In Office365CalendarService, the tokenResponse.data is spread into o365AuthCredentials, preserving all fields. The finding misreads what the code does.
